course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 07 teaches WHERE filtering from comparison operators to AND/OR/NOT, ranges, lists, patterns, NULL checks, boolean logic and complex predicates.
outcomes: Combine predicates with AND, OR and NOT
Use BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and IS NULL
Reason about NULL and three-valued logic

modules.title: WHERE Clause and Filtering
modules.goal: Write precise predicates and avoid NULL and precedence traps.

topics.title: Introduction to WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE rows ko filter karta hai — sirf matching rows result me aate hain.
topics.pro: WHERE is a row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; it keeps only rows whose predicate is true.
points: False or unknown rows are removed.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Filtering Rows
topics.simple: Filter lagane se result chhota aur relevant hota hai.
topics.pro: A predicate is a boolean expression; rows with a true result pass, while false and NULL results are discarded.
points: A predicate returns true, false or unknown.
Unknown behaves like false for filtering.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 60;

topics.title: Equality (=)
topics.simple: = exact match check karta hai.
topics.pro: The equality operator compares two values and returns true only when they are equal; NULL never equals anything.
points: Double quotes are identifiers, not strings.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';

topics.title: Inequality (!= and <>)
topics.simple: Not equal ke liye <> ya != use karo.
topics.pro: Both <> and != mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks <> 80;

topics.title: Greater Than and Less Than
topics.simple: > bada aur < chhota compare karta hai.
topics.pro: > and < compare values using the type’s ordering; they work for numbers, dates and text under the database collation.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Greater Than or Equal and Less Than or Equal
topics.simple: >= aur <= boundary value ko bhi include karte hain.
topics.pro: >= keeps values greater than or equal to the boundary; <= keeps values less than or equal to it.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

topics.title: AND
topics.simple: AND tab true hota hai jab dono conditions true hon.
topics.pro: AND combines predicates with logical conjunction; both sides must be true for the row to pass.
points: One false side rejects the row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 AND marks <= 90;

topics.title: OR
topics.simple: OR tab true hota hai jab koi ek condition true ho.
topics.pro: OR combines predicates with logical disjunction; at least one side must be true for the row to pass.
points: Two false sides reject the row.
NULL on both sides yields unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera';

topics.title: NOT
topics.simple: NOT condition ko ulta karta hai.
topics.pro: NOT negates a boolean predicate; NOT true is false, NOT false is true and NOT unknown is unknown.
points: NOT is not the same as !=.
Negating a NULL predicate stays unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE NOT (marks < 60);
example.output: Students with 60 or more, excluding NULL marks.

topics.title: Combining AND, OR and NOT
topics.simple: Mixed conditions me precedence aur parentheses bahut important hain.
topics.pro: Mixed predicates combine with NOT, AND and OR; AND binds tighter than OR, so parentheses should state the intended grouping.
points: NOT applies to the expression that follows.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN
topics.simple: BETWEEN inclusive range check karta hai.
topics.pro: BETWEEN low AND high is inclusive on both ends; NOT BETWEEN keeps values outside the range.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

topics.title: IN and NOT IN
topics.simple: IN list me se koi match check karta hai.
topics.pro: IN tests membership in a value list; NOT IN tests exclusion, with a dangerous NULL behaviour.
points: IN is shorthand for several ORs.
NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows.
The list values must be comparable.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name IN ('Aarav', 'Meera', 'Kabir');

topics.title: LIKE and NOT LIKE
topics.simple: LIKE pattern matching karta hai, NOT LIKE ulta.
topics.pro: LIKE matches text against a pattern with % and _ wildcards; it is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL, while ILIKE is case-insensitive.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

topics.title: Percent Wildcard
topics.simple: % kisi bhi length ke characters ko match karta hai.
topics.pro: The % wildcard matches zero or more characters in a LIKE pattern.
points: A% matches names starting with A.
A leading % usually prevents a plain index scan.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '%a%';

topics.title: Underscore Wildcard
topics.simple: _ exactly ek character match karta hai.
topics.pro: The _ wildcard matches exactly one character, so it is useful for fixed-position patterns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '_a%';
example.output: Names whose second character is a.

topics.title: IS NULL
topics.simple: NULL check karne ke liye IS NULL use karo, = NULL nahi.
topics.pro: IS NULL is the only reliable null test; equality with NULL returns unknown and filters every row out.
points: IS NULL is the correct predicate.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;

topics.title: IS NOT NULL
topics.simple: IS NOT NULL aise rows deta hai jahan value present ho.
topics.pro: IS NOT NULL keeps rows where the column has a real value rather than NULL.
points: It is the negation of IS NULL.
It does not treat empty string as NULL.
Use it before comparing optional columns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: Boolean Filtering
topics.simple: Boolean column ko seedha WHERE me use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A boolean column is itself a predicate; WHERE active keeps true, WHERE NOT active keeps false, and NULL is excluded from both.
points: Use IS NOT TRUE to include NULL.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM users WHERE active;

topics.title: Operator Precedence
topics.simple: Comparison pehle, phir NOT, phir AND, phir OR.
topics.pro: Comparison operators bind tighter than NOT, NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR; rely on parentheses when mixing.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 OR name = 'Aarav' AND marks > 60;

topics.title: Parentheses
topics.simple: Parentheses se condition ka group clear karo.
topics.pro: Parentheses override precedence and make the intended logic readable; they are the cheapest way to prevent a filter bug.
points: Group OR before AND when needed.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: Case Sensitivity and ILIKE
topics.simple: PostgreSQL text comparison case-sensitive hai; ILIKE case-insensitive match deta hai.
topics.pro: LIKE and = compare text case-sensitively under the collation; ILIKE lowercases both sides for matching, and LOWER(name) is the portable alternative.
points: LOWER() can match but may not use a plain index.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name ILIKE 'aarav';

topics.title: Escaping Wildcards
topics.simple: Literal % ya _ match karna ho to ESCAPE use karo.
topics.pro: A backslash escapes % and _ in a LIKE pattern when ESCAPE is declared; without escaping, the wildcard keeps its special meaning.

example.sql: SELECT code FROM items WHERE code LIKE 'A\_%' ESCAPE '\';
example.output: Codes starting with the literal A_.

topics.title: Complex WHERE Conditions
topics.simple: Real filters me multiple AND, OR, IN, LIKE aur NULL checks combine hote hain.
topics.pro: A complex predicate should be built in layers: isolate each rule, parenthesize OR groups, and test the row count before trusting the result.
points: Write one rule at a time.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE 'M%') AND marks BETWEEN 60 AND 95 AND email IS NOT NULL;
example.output: Matching names with marks in range and a known email.

topics.title: Practical Student Filtering
topics.simple: Ab multiple filters ko mila kar ek useful student report banao.
topics.pro: A production filter combines range, membership, pattern and null checks while keeping each predicate readable and index-friendly.
points: Avoid leading wildcards on large tables.
Verify the row count before shipping.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND name LIKE 'A%' AND email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY marks DESC;
example.output: Students in range whose name starts with A and have an email.

learn.q: What does WHERE do?
learn.why: WHERE keeps rows whose predicate is true.

learn.q: Which operator tests equality?
learn.why: SQL uses a single = for equality.

learn.q: Which two operators mean not equal?
learn.why: Both are accepted; <> is standard SQL.

learn.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
learn.why: BETWEEN low AND high includes both boundaries.

learn.q: What is IN shorthand for?
learn.why: name IN (a, b) matches either value.

learn.q: Is LIKE case-sensitive in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is case-insensitive.

learn.q: Which operator is case-insensitive?
learn.why: ILIKE lowercases both sides for matching.

learn.q: What does % match in a LIKE pattern?
learn.why: % matches zero or more characters.

learn.q: What does _ match in a LIKE pattern?
learn.why: _ is a single-character wildcard.

learn.q: How do you test for NULL?
learn.why: Equality with NULL is unknown and never matches.

learn.q: What does name = NULL return?
learn.why: The comparison is unknown for every row.

learn.q: What does NOT IN (1, NULL) return?
learn.why: Each comparison with NULL becomes unknown, so the NOT IN predicate never passes.

learn.q: Which binds tighter: AND or OR?
learn.why: AND has higher precedence than OR.

learn.q: Why use parentheses in mixed conditions?
learn.why: Parentheses override precedence and prevent logic bugs.

learn.q: What does WHERE active keep?
learn.why: A boolean predicate passes only when it is true.

learn.q: What does WHERE active IS NOT TRUE keep?
learn.why: IS NOT TRUE is true for false and unknown.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in WHERE?
learn.why: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT defines the alias.

learn.q: Can WHERE use aggregate functions?
learn.why: Aggregates are not allowed in WHERE; use HAVING after grouping.

learn.q: Which pattern matches names starting with A?
learn.why: A% means A followed by any sequence.

learn.q: Which pattern matches a second character of a?
learn.why: _ matches the first character and a is the second.

interview.q: What is WHERE?
interview.answer: A row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; only rows whose predicate is true pass.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

interview.q: What comparison operators does SQL provide?
interview.answer: =, <>, !=, >, <, >= and <=, plus BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and IS NULL predicates.

interview.q: What is the difference between <> and !=?
interview.answer: Both mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.

interview.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
interview.answer: Yes, both the low and high boundaries are included.

interview.q: What is IN equivalent to?
interview.answer: A chain of OR equality comparisons, such as x = a OR x = b.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN with NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: Every comparison with NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate can return no rows unexpectedly.

interview.q: What is the difference between LIKE and ILIKE?
interview.answer: LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is case-insensitive in PostgreSQL.

interview.q: What do % and _ mean in LIKE?
interview.answer: % matches any sequence of characters; _ matches exactly one character.

interview.q: How do you match a literal % or _?
interview.answer: Escape it with a backslash and declare ESCAPE, for example LIKE A\_% ESCAPE '\'.

interview.q: How do you test for NULL?
interview.answer: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches.

interview.q: What is three-valued logic?
interview.answer: SQL predicates can be true, false or unknown; unknown arises from NULL comparisons and is filtered like false.

interview.q: How does WHERE treat a boolean column?
interview.answer: The column is itself the predicate: WHERE active keeps true rows.

interview.q: How do you include false and NULL boolean rows?
interview.answer: Use WHERE active IS NOT TRUE; WHERE NOT active keeps only false.

interview.q: What is the precedence of NOT, AND and OR?
interview.answer: NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR.

interview.q: Why use parentheses?
interview.answer: They override precedence and document the intended grouping.

interview.q: Can a SELECT alias be used in WHERE?
interview.answer: No, because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT.

interview.q: Can WHERE use functions?
interview.answer: Yes, but a function on a column can prevent a plain index scan.

interview.q: Why can a leading % hurt performance?
interview.answer: It prevents a normal B-tree index scan because the pattern has no fixed prefix.

interview.q: How do you filter a date range?
interview.answer: Use >= start AND < next_day for a half-open range, or BETWEEN for inclusive dates.

logic.q: Why does name = NULL return no rows?
logic.answer: Equality with an unknown value is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true rows.

logic.q: Why does NOT IN (1, NULL) return no rows?
logic.answer: Each comparison against NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate never becomes true.

logic.q: Why does AND bind tighter than OR?
logic.answer: SQL gives AND higher precedence, so a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c).

logic.q: Why use parentheses even when precedence is known?
logic.answer: They document intent and prevent a later edit from changing the logic.
It expands to low <= x AND x <= high, including both boundaries.
It compares text under the collation without case folding; ILIKE performs the case-insensitive match.
It cannot use a plain B-tree index on the original text; it may need a scan or a special index.

logic.q: Why can LOWER(name) prevent an index scan?
logic.answer: A plain index on name does not index LOWER(name); use an expression index if needed.

logic.q: Why does WHERE active exclude NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL boolean is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true.

logic.q: Why does IS NOT TRUE include NULL?
logic.answer: It is true for both false and unknown values.

logic.q: Why does a leading % hurt performance?
logic.answer: The pattern has no fixed prefix, so a normal B-tree cannot seek to a starting point.

logic.q: Why does _ match exactly one character?
logic.answer: It is the single-character wildcard in LIKE patterns.
It tells LIKE which character makes the next wildcard literal.

logic.q: Why can a SELECT alias not be used in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the surviving rows are grouped and aggregated.

debug.title: NULL with equality
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email = NULL;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;

debug.title: Double-quoted string
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = "Aarav";
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';

debug.title: Reversed BETWEEN
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 90 AND 60;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

debug.title: NOT IN with NULL
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks NOT IN (60, NULL);
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks NOT IN (60) AND marks IS NOT NULL;
debug.expected: Rows not equal to 60 with known marks.

debug.title: Boolean NULL
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM users WHERE active = NULL;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM users WHERE active IS NULL;

debug.title: Missing parentheses
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera' AND marks > 80;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

debug.title: Trailing AND
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 AND;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 AND email IS NOT NULL;

debug.title: Aggregate in WHERE
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students GROUP BY name HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
debug.error: aggregate functions are not allowed in WHERE

debug.title: Alias in WHERE
debug.broken: SELECT name AS n FROM students WHERE n = 'Aarav';
debug.fix: SELECT name AS n FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';

debug.title: Unescaped underscore
debug.broken: SELECT code FROM items WHERE code LIKE 'A_%';
debug.fix: SELECT code FROM items WHERE code LIKE 'A\_%' ESCAPE '\';
debug.error: Matches any second character, not a literal underscore
